title: Our Hearts Are the Same: The Hidden Christians of Urakami
subtitle: Urakami and the Gotō islands, Nagasaki; disclosure, arrest, exile and return, 1865–1873
intro: For about 250 years after Christianity was banned in 1614, families in the villages around Nagasaki, in Urakami, Sotome and the Gotō islands, kept a faith that the state believed it had destroyed. They were registered at Buddhist temples, stepped on Christian images when the magistrate's officers came round each year, and kept their prayers, baptisms and a church calendar in the hands of their own lay leaders. Their survival depended on one condition: that nobody outside knew for certain.

On 17 March 1865 a group from Urakami walked into the new French church at Ōura and broke that condition on purpose. What followed was the last great persecution of Christians in Japan. The refusal of Buddhist funerals in 1867 exposed the village; the shogun's magistrate raided its secret chapels; the new Meiji government renewed the ban and, between 1868 and 1870, scattered about 3,400 Urakami Christians among some twenty domains, where about 600 died. Western diplomats protested, the Iwakura Mission met the issue in America and Europe, and in February 1873 the notice boards banning Christianity came down. The exiles returned.

The honest record is lopsided. No diary by a villager from these years has been found. The villagers' only firsthand written voice here is Takagi Sen'emon's memorandum, written later and known through modern study; the woman who spoke first at Ōura survives only in a priest's letter and church memory. Almost everything else was written by people outside the community: the French missionary to whom they disclosed themselves, the magistrates who interrogated them, the Japanese ministers who exiled them, and the British and American diplomats who argued about them. Most of these sources are letters, dispatches, protocols and decrees rather than diaries, and they are tagged that way.

Read together, they show the same act described in incompatible terms. To Petitjean it was a resurrection; to the magistrate, a crime; to Sanjō Sanetomi, insubordination; to Parkes, persecution of people who shared his faith; to a Japanese official memorandum, a peaceful removal in which no one was arrested. The figures move too: 63, 65 or 68 arrested; 4,010 sentenced; Satow's 'some four thousand'; 3,394 exiled; 2,800 reported to Parliament; 613 or more dead.

The chapter ends with a group the diplomats never wrote about: the hidden Christians who did not join the Church when it became legal. For them, concealment had stopped being only a disguise and had become a tradition of its own. Their practices are described here only in outline.
calendar_note: Japan used a lunisolar calendar until the end of 1872: the 3rd day of the 12th month of Meiji 5 became 1 January 1873. Western writers (Petitjean, Satow, the diplomats) dated their letters in the Gregorian calendar, while Japanese records use era, month and day (Genji, Keiō, Meiji). date_iso always gives the Gregorian date. The 1865 disclosure fell in the 2nd month of Genji 2; the Urakami raid in the night of the 13th–14th day of the 6th month of Keiō 3 (14–15 July 1867); the Osaka meetings of May 1868 in the 4th and intercalary 4th months of Keiō 4. The bans' removal on 24 February 1873 is already a Gregorian date. The hidden communities themselves kept a church calendar of 1634 adapted to the lunar months, so their feast days drifted against the European calendar.
seam: These records describe a community that lasted only while its secret held, and was then exposed by its own decision to trust an outsider. Once the secret was out, it was not the villagers who decided what it meant: magistrates, ministers and envoys each wrote it down in their own terms, and the people at the centre left almost no written words. As in Le Guin's 'The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas', the question these papers raise is what a hidden arrangement protects and who pays when it ends. The communities that chose to stay hidden after 1873 suggest that a world kept in secret long enough becomes a reality in its own right.

eyes.name: Bernard-Thadée Petitjean
eyes.role: French priest of the Paris Foreign Missions Society (MEP), aged 35 in 1865; priest of the new Ōura church in the Nagasaki foreign settlement; consecrated bishop and vicar apostolic of Japan in 1866
eyes.side: Catholic mission; French subject under treaty protection
eyes.where: Ōura church on the hill above the Nagasaki foreign settlement
eyes.vantage_label: the outsider to whom the secret was disclosed
eyes.authenticity: His letters to his superiors (notably to Mgr Prudence Girard in Yokohama) and to Paris survive in the MEP archives; they were printed in mission periodicals and gathered by Francisque Marnas in La 'Religion de Jésus' ressuscitée au Japon (1896; revised 1931) and later in a Japanese compilation of his letters. The French originals are public domain; no pre-1929 English translation could be verified for this chapter, so his words are given here only in paraphrase.
eyes.bio: Petitjean came to Japan expecting to serve foreigners in the treaty ports and to search, if he could, for traces of the Christians of the seventeenth century. Within a month of the Ōura church opening, villagers from Urakami chose him as the person to whom they would reveal themselves. His letters are the main written record of what the hidden communities preserved and how they tested the newcomer, and they also show how his insistence on full Catholic practice helped bring the community into the open.

sources.title: Japan Tourism Agency multilingual commentary: Discovery of the Hidden Christians (PDF)
Takayama Ukon site: The Discovery of the 'Hidden Christians' of Japan (summarising Petitjean's letters)
Thomas W. Burkman, 'The Urakami Incidents and the Struggle for Religious Toleration in Early Meiji Japan', Japanese Journal of Religious Studies 1/2-3 (1974)

eyes.name: Isabelina Sugimoto Yuri
eyes.life: born c. 1813; death date not established here
eyes.role: No surviving firsthand account found. A farming woman of Urakami village, about 52 in 1865 according to Japanese accounts, remembered as the speaker on 17 March 1865
eyes.where: Urakami village, north of Nagasaki; at Ōura church on 17 March 1865
eyes.vantage_label: a hidden Christian who chose to speak
eyes.form: known only from the missionary's letter and later church tradition
eyes.authenticity: No writing by her is known. Petitjean's letter of 18 March 1865 describes an unnamed woman of about forty or fifty; her name, baptismal name and age come from later Japanese church tradition and local histories.
eyes.bio: The villagers who approached Petitjean had to decide, on very little evidence, whether this foreigner belonged to the faith they had kept in secret for over two centuries. The words remembered as hers, that their hearts were the same as his, are the moment the concealment was broken on purpose. She is present here only through other people's records.

sources.title: Japan Tourism Agency multilingual commentary: Discovery of the Hidden Christians (PDF)
Wikipedia: Urakami Yoban Kuzure (chronology with Japanese sources)

eyes.name: Takagi Sen'emon (baptised Dominico)
eyes.role: Urakami farmer and lay leader, aged about 43 in 1867; arrested in the raid of July 1867 and the one prisoner recorded as refusing to recant; later exiled
eyes.where: Urakami; Nagasaki magistrate's prison; exile in western Japan
eyes.vantage_label: a villager who was arrested and exiled
eyes.authenticity: His Oboegaki ('memorandum'), a later personal account of the persecution, survives and has been analysed by Takagi Yoshiko (2013). The date of composition and the full text could not be checked for this chapter; entries draw on published summaries of his story and are marked accordingly.
eyes.bio: Takagi kept a secret chapel in his own house; a government spy's floor plan of it survives. When the village's refusal of Buddhist funerals brought officials to ask questions, he declared his faith openly. He is the rare villager whose own written account exists, though written after the events.

sources.title: Takagi Yoshiko, Takagi Sen'emon ni kansuru kenkyū: 'Oboegaki' no bunseki o chūshin ni shite (Shibunkaku, 2013), NDL record
Japan Tourism Agency multilingual commentary: Urakami and the Fourth Urakami Crackdown
Japan Tourism Agency multilingual commentary: the Fourth Urakami Crackdown (PDF)

eyes.name: Okabe Nagatsune (Suruga no kami)
eyes.role: Nagasaki magistrate (bugyō) at the time of the Third Urakami Crackdown, 1856
eyes.vantage_label: the state's interrogator, a decade before
eyes.authenticity: The record of his interrogation of the arrested chōkata Kichizō is preserved among the Nagasaki magistrate's papers and is used in modern histories; it was not read directly for this chapter.
eyes.bio: His record of the 1856 arrests is one of the few official documents to describe the hidden community's practices from the inside of an interrogation room. It shows that the authorities knew something was being kept in Urakami long before 1865.

sources.title: Japan Tourism Agency multilingual commentary: Bastian and the hidden communities (PDF)

eyes.name: Tokunaga Masayoshi (Iwami no kami)
eyes.role: The 125th Nagasaki magistrate, who ordered the raid of July 1867
eyes.vantage_label: the official who made the arrests
eyes.form: official records of the magistrate's office
eyes.authenticity: The arrests are documented in the magistrate's papers and in diplomatic correspondence; numbers differ between sources (63, 65 or 68 at first, rising to 83).
eyes.bio: Tokunaga acted on reports from spies sent after the funeral dispute. Foreign diplomats protested to him within days, and the American minister reported that he had acted on his own responsibility.

sources.title: Japan Tourism Agency multilingual commentary: Urakami and the Fourth Urakami Crackdown
Japan Tourism Agency multilingual commentary: the Fourth Urakami Crackdown (PDF)
FRUS 1867 pt II, doc. 48: Van Valkenburgh to Seward, No. 44, 23 Aug 1867

eyes.name: Robert B. Van Valkenburgh
eyes.role: United States Minister Resident in Japan, 1866–69
eyes.where: Yedo and Yokohama; met the Nagasaki governors in 1867
eyes.vantage_label: foreign envoy, reporting from the capital
eyes.authenticity: Printed by the US government in the annual Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs (FRUS); public domain.
eyes.bio: A former Union general and congressman, he wrote cautious dispatches that passed on the missionaries' accounts but advised against pressing Japan too hard. His figures for the arrests and sentences are among the earliest Western numbers.

sources.title: FRUS 1867 pt II, doc. 48: Van Valkenburgh to Seward, No. 44, 23 Aug 1867
FRUS 1867 pt II, doc. 60: Van Valkenburgh to Seward, No. 63, 12 Nov 1867
FRUS 1868 pt I, doc. 361: Van Valkenburgh to Seward, No. 83, 15 Aug 1868

eyes.name: Léon Roches
eyes.role: French minister plenipotentiary in Japan, 1864–68, close adviser to the last shogun
eyes.vantage_label: protecting power, negotiating with the shogun
eyes.authenticity: His dispatches are in the French diplomatic archives; they were not consulted for this chapter, and his intervention is given from secondary histories.
eyes.bio: Because the Ōura priests were French, the arrests became a French question. Roches used his standing with Tokugawa Yoshinobu to obtain the prisoners' release under surveillance, a reprieve that lasted only until the shogunate fell.

sources.title: Thomas W. Burkman, 'The Urakami Incidents and the Struggle for Religious Toleration in Early Meiji Japan', Japanese Journal of Religious Studies 1/2-3 (1974)

eyes.name: Ernest Mason Satow
eyes.role: Japanese secretary of the British legation, aged 25 in 1868; interpreter at Parkes's meetings with the new government
eyes.where: Osaka and Kyoto, spring and summer 1868
eyes.form: memoir (written later) based on his diaries
eyes.authenticity: A Diplomat in Japan (1921) was written decades later from his diaries, which survive in the UK National Archives (PRO 30/33). Quoted here from the 1921 text.
eyes.bio: Satow interpreted as Parkes argued with the Meiji leaders about the anti-Christian notice and the Urakami villagers. His account records both the arguments and his own later judgement that the protests changed little.

sources.title: Ernest Satow, A Diplomat in Japan (1921), Project Gutenberg #43541

eyes.name: Sir Harry Smith Parkes
eyes.role: British Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary in Japan, 1865–83
eyes.authenticity: His dispatches were printed in British parliamentary papers; the protocol of the 19 January 1870 conference used here is the version printed by the US government in FRUS 1870.
eyes.bio: Parkes led the foreign representatives' protests in 1868 and again when the mass deportation began in January 1870. The Japanese protocol of their argument records his words beside the prime minister's, the clearest place where the two framings of the problem meet.

sources.title: FRUS 1870, doc. 282: De Long to Fish, with protocol of the 19 January 1870 conference
Hansard, House of Commons, 18 March 1870, vol. 200 cc203-4
Ernest Satow, A Diplomat in Japan (1921), Project Gutenberg #43541

eyes.name: Ōkuma Shigenobu (then Ōkuma Hachitarō)
eyes.role: Young Hizen samurai and Meiji official, aged 30 in 1868; later prime minister
eyes.authenticity: Ōkuma's own later reminiscences were not consulted for this chapter; he appears here only through Satow's record.
eyes.bio: Ōkuma had studied with an American missionary in Nagasaki and argued the government's case against Parkes. His claim to know the subject from reading the Bible shows that the Meiji leaders were not ignorant of Christianity; they judged it a political danger.

sources.title: Ernest Satow, A Diplomat in Japan (1921), Project Gutenberg #43541

eyes.name: Kido Takayoshi
eyes.role: Chōshū leader and Meiji councillor, aged 35 in 1868; later a vice-ambassador of the Iwakura Mission
eyes.where: Kyoto and Osaka; Nagasaki in July 1868; abroad 1871–73
eyes.vantage_label: the official who carried out the first deportation
eyes.authenticity: Kido kept a diary from 1868 to 1877 (Japanese edition; English translation by Brown and Hirota, 1983–86). The diary was not read directly for this chapter, so his entries here rest on histories and are marked secondhand.
eyes.bio: Kido went to Nagasaki in 1868 and arranged the sending of 114 leading Urakami Christians to Hagi, Tsuwano and Fukuyama. Four years later, as a vice-ambassador abroad, he met Western objections to the persecution at first hand.

sources.title: The Diary of Kido Takayoshi, tr. Sidney DeVere Brown and Akiko Hirota, vol. 1 (Univ. of Tokyo Press, 1983), CiNii record
Japan Tourism Agency multilingual commentary: Urakami and the Fourth Urakami Crackdown

eyes.name: Sanjō Sanetomi
eyes.role: Court noble and head of the Meiji government (Minister of the Right in 1870, called 'prime minister' in the Western protocol)
eyes.authenticity: His words of 19 January 1870 survive in the protocol printed in FRUS 1870; the proclamations of 1868 and 1873 are Dajōkan records held in the National Archives of Japan.
eyes.bio: Sanjō presided over the meeting at which Parkes protested the deportations and gave the government's answer: the villagers were being moved for disobedience, not belief. The same government removed the notice boards in 1873.

sources.title: FRUS 1870, doc. 282: De Long to Fish, with protocol of the 19 January 1870 conference
Japan Tourism Agency multilingual commentary: the lifting of the ban (PDF)

eyes.name: Charles E. De Long
eyes.role: United States Minister Resident in Japan, 1869–72
eyes.vantage_label: foreign envoy, forwarding both sides' papers
eyes.authenticity: Printed in FRUS 1870; public domain. Includes translated Japanese memoranda whose authorship he could only guess.
eyes.bio: De Long joined the January 1870 protests and then forwarded to Washington a Japanese official account of the deportation that denied any force had been used. His dispatches set the two versions side by side without settling them.

sources.title: FRUS 1870, doc. 282: De Long to Fish, with protocol of the 19 January 1870 conference
FRUS 1870, doc. 286: De Long to Fish, 12 Apr 1870, with Japanese memorandum

eyes.name: Kume Kunitake
eyes.role: Saga-born scholar, aged 32, official recorder of the Iwakura Mission, 1871–73
eyes.vantage_label: abroad, seeing the faith in its own countries
eyes.authenticity: Tokumei zenken taishi Bei-Ō kairan jikki (1878), five volumes, compiled from the mission's notes; modern English translation (Healey and Tsuzuki, 2002) is copyrighted, so summary only.
eyes.bio: Kume watched Christianity as a living public religion in America and Europe while the mission heard complaints about the Urakami exiles. His record treats the faith as something to be understood as part of Western civilisation, a very different frame from the notice boards at home.

sources.title: History of Japanese in NY: Christian Organizations (Iwakura Mission in New York, citing Kume)

entries.headline: Third Urakami crackdown: the chōkata Kichizō is questioned
entries.digest: Acting on informers, the magistrate's men arrested Urakami leaders, among them two physicians of the Kataoka family and the chōkata Kichizō, keeper of the community's church calendar. Okabe's interrogation record set down what the group did; several of the prisoners died in prison. Holy images were confiscated, and villagers reportedly took a small Maria-Kannon figure to the Tenpukuji temple for safekeeping.
entries.source_note: Japan Tourism Agency commentary (MLIT 001561259) summarising the magistrate's record.

entries.headline: Night visits and four secret chapels
entries.digest: Petitjean and Father Laucaigne began to visit Urakami secretly after dark, since priests were confined to the foreign settlement. The villagers built four makeshift chapels in their houses, one of them in Takagi Sen'emon's home. Word spread to communities in Sotome and the Gotō islands, who also came to Ōura.
entries.source_note: Burkman 1974 (from Petitjean's letters via Marnas and later histories); MLIT 001561261 for Takagi's house chapel.

entries.date_display: handed down from the 17th century; recorded in the 19th–20th centuries
entries.headline: Bastian's calendar and the promise of the black ships
entries.digest: The communities Petitjean was meeting kept their feast and fast days by a church calendar of 1634 adapted to the Japanese lunar calendar, attributed to a Japanese catechist called Bastian, martyred in 1659. In Sotome, prophecies credited to him were passed down orally: after seven generations confessors would come on large black ships, and Christians would one day sing their prayers aloud. Believers later read 1865 as the fulfilment.
entries.source_note: MLIT commentary 001561259. The prophecies are oral tradition recorded later, not part of Petitjean's letters; presented as tradition, not fact.

entries.headline: The 'French temple' opens on the hill at Ōura
entries.digest: The church built for the foreign community at Ōura, dedicated to the twenty-six martyrs of 1597, was consecrated. Its sign over the door read tenshudō, 'church', in Japanese characters. Curious Japanese came to look at it, and the priests could not tell who among them might be more than curious.
entries.source_note: Consecration date per MLIT commentary and Japanese church chronologies; Ueno Hikoma's photograph c. 1865 shows the sign.

entries.headline: Fourteen or fifteen villagers enter and test the priest
entries.digest: About midday a group of fourteen or fifteen people from Urakami came into the church while Petitjean was there. As he knelt, a woman of perhaps forty or fifty came close and told him that all of them shared his heart, and then asked where the image of Santa Maria was. He led them to the statue of the Virgin and Child, and they asked him further questions that seemed meant to test whether he was the kind of priest their ancestors had known.
entries.source_note: Petitjean to Mgr Girard, letter dated 18 March 1865, as summarised in MLIT commentary 001561260 and Burkman 1974.

entries.headline: The words remembered as Yuri's: our hearts are the same
entries.digest: Church tradition identifies the speaker as Isabelina Sugimoto Yuri of Urakami, about 52. Speaking meant risking the village: Christianity was still forbidden by law, and the 1856 arrests were within living memory. The question about Santa Maria was the community's test of whether this priest kept the old faith.
entries.form: church tradition based on a missionary letter
entries.source_note: Name and age from later Japanese tradition and local histories (see Wikipedia chronology); the words are known only through Petitjean's letter.

entries.headline: Petitjean writes that the old Christians are alive
entries.digest: The day after, Petitjean wrote to his superior in Yokohama that his doubts had vanished at the name of the Virgin. He concluded that he was standing before descendants of the Christians of the early seventeenth century, whom Europe had believed wiped out. The letter was the first written account of the disclosure, set down by the outsider rather than by the villagers.
entries.source_note: Letter of 18 March 1865, per MLIT commentary 001561260; printed in Marnas (1896).

entries.headline: What they kept: prayers, a contrition text, a baptism
entries.digest: Through long interviews Petitjean and his colleagues wrote down more than twenty words the villagers used for baptism and checked their meanings with them. He praised a 1603 text on contrition that the community had preserved. After consulting Rome, the missionaries judged that, with a few exceptions, the baptisms performed by the hidden leaders were valid.
entries.source_note: Letter of 30 June 1865 as summarised on the Takayama Ukon site from the compiled letters of Mgr Petitjean; content not read in the original.

entries.headline: Hidden groups are not one community
entries.digest: Petitjean wrote about rivalries among the hidden groups, who had developed separate lines of leaders and traditions over two centuries. Some were eager to accept the missionaries; others were wary of a foreign priest who might overturn their own customs. The split foreshadowed the later division between those who joined the Church and those who did not.
entries.source_note: Letter of 29 January 1866 as summarised on the Takayama Ukon site.

entries.headline: The funeral dispute: burying their own dead
entries.digest: Urakami families buried their dead without calling the monk of Shōtokuji, the Buddhist temple where every household was registered. When the village headman questioned them they declared that they were Christians, and Takagi and others repeated this openly before the magistrate's office. The perplexed magistrate sent them home, but spies were sent to watch the village and report to Edo.
entries.form: later histories drawing on official papers and Takagi's account
entries.source_note: MLIT R1-00790 and 001561261; Wikipedia chronology. The exact month varies between accounts.

entries.headline: No outward Buddhist rites, the priests insist
entries.digest: The missionaries taught that a Christian could not take even outward part in Buddhist rites. For people who had survived by appearing Buddhist, this turned the old disguise into a sin. The refusal of temple funerals followed directly.
entries.source_note: Burkman 1974, drawing on missionary correspondence.

entries.headline: The magistrate's raid on the secret chapels
entries.digest: In the middle of the night about 170 of the magistrate's men raided the house chapels of Urakami. Sixty-eight people were taken, Takagi Sen'emon among them, and more arrests followed, bringing the total to 83. The prisoners were held in harsh conditions and pressed to renounce their faith.
entries.form: official records of the magistrate's office
entries.source_note: MLIT R1-00790 and 001561261; Wikipedia chronology (14 July, old calendar 13th of 6th month).

entries.headline: Under pressure, all but one recant
entries.digest: Imprisoned and tortured, the arrested villagers one by one promised to give up their faith. Takagi is recorded as the one who would not. His later memorandum is the only account written by one of the prisoners themselves.
entries.form: memorandum written later and later histories
entries.source_note: Wikipedia chronology and MLIT summaries; Takagi's Oboegaki per Takagi Yoshiko (2013). Exact wording of the memorandum not checked.

entries.headline: The American minister asks for the prisoners' release
entries.digest: Van Valkenburgh met the governors of Nagasaki twice to ask that the prisoners be freed. They refused, saying the villagers had been arrested as criminals under Japanese law. He also wrote to the Japanese foreign ministry, and hoped Washington would approve his conduct.
entries.quote: They declined, having arrested them as criminals under the laws of Japan
entries.source_note: FRUS 1867 pt II, doc. 48 (dispatch of 23 Aug 1867).

entries.headline: First American report of the arrests
entries.digest: Writing to Seward, he relayed what he had confirmed with Bishop Petitjean: a night arrest of men, women and children in a valley about four miles from Nagasaki. He understood that there had been no torture and that the governors had promised to care for the families. He judged that the governor had acted on his own responsibility.
entries.quote: the governor, in the night time, caused the arrest of 63 men, women, and children, in the little valley of Owri Kami
entries.source_note: FRUS 1867 pt II, doc. 48.

entries.headline: Roches puts the case to the last shogun
entries.digest: The French minister raised the arrests with Tokugawa Yoshinobu at Osaka Castle. The shogunate gave way: the prisoners were released, but on condition of police surveillance, and the French priests were forbidden to contact them.
entries.source_note: Date per Wikipedia chronology; terms per Burkman 1974.

entries.date_display: 12 November 1867 (enclosing an account dated Nagasaki, 16 September 1867)
entries.headline: The missionaries' account reaches Washington
entries.digest: Van Valkenburgh forwarded a letter from Bishop Petitjean and an account written in Nagasaki in September by one of the French priests. It said about 65 villagers were still held in cramped conditions, that promised releases had not happened, and that their resistance was religious, not political. The minister himself thought it a bad moment to push Japan further.
entries.quote: Our cause is the cause of God.
entries.form: dated diplomatic dispatches with missionary enclosure
entries.source_note: FRUS 1867 pt II, doc. 60.

entries.place: Tateyama office of the Nagasaki magistrate
entries.headline: A night summons and a refusal
entries.digest: Kawazu Sukekuni, the 126th magistrate, called Takagi to the Tateyama office at night and tried in person to talk him out of his faith. Takagi refused. Within weeks the shogunate itself collapsed, and the question passed to the new imperial government.
entries.form: later histories drawing on Takagi's account
entries.source_note: MLIT R1-00790 and 001561261; date inferred from Kawazu's term as magistrate.

entries.headline: New government, same ban: the notice boards go up
entries.digest: The new imperial government issued five public notices to be posted throughout the country. One of them renewed the prohibition of Christianity, calling it a pernicious sect. The boards stood in every town until 1873.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia chronology; MLIT 001561262 (boards erected 1868, removed 1873); Satow's account of the 'recently published edict'.

entries.headline: Ministers and daimyō asked what to do about Urakami
entries.digest: Satow recorded that the emperor's ministers and the daimyō had been informed that Christianity was spreading at Urakami and asked for their views. The question was being treated as a matter of state security. He noted that his informant was not well informed on the details.
entries.quote: Christianity was on the increase at Urakami, a village near Nagasaki
entries.form: memoir (written later) based on his diaries
entries.source_note: Satow, A Diplomat in Japan (1921), ch. XXXII.

entries.headline: An imperial council decides on deportation
entries.digest: Meeting in Osaka, the government's leaders decided that the Urakami Christians should be removed from their village and dispersed. Kido was among those who argued for firm measures. Foreign protests were weighed, and the result was exile rather than execution.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia chronology (Gonoi; Iechika 1998).

entries.headline: Date Munenari admits the wording was wrong
entries.digest: On the day Parkes landed, he raised the new anti-Christian notice with Date Munenari. Date admitted that the wording was objectionable and said he had kept the board off the public posts at Osaka and Hyōgo, the open ports. It was a small, local concealment of the ban from foreign eyes.
entries.form: memoir (written later) based on his diaries
entries.source_note: Satow (1921), ch. XXXI; day given as Parkes's arrival.

entries.headline: Parkes argues toleration with the new ministers
entries.digest: At a long meeting at the Nishi Hongwanji with Sanjō, Date, Gotō, Kido and others, Parkes protested the notice. The ministers defended the ban but agreed that calling Christianity a pernicious sect had been an error and would be changed. Satow recorded Parkes's argument in a single line.
entries.quote: Sir Harry responded that religious toleration was a mark of civilization
entries.source_note: Satow (1921), ch. XXXI.

entries.headline: Ōkuma says he has read the Bible
entries.digest: When Parkes raised the subject again, Iwakura joined the ministers and the young Hizen samurai Ōkuma argued the government's side. Satow, meeting him for the first time, noted that Ōkuma claimed to know the subject because he had read the Bible, having studied with an American missionary in Nagasaki. The government's case was that the faith threatened public order, not that it was unknown.
entries.quote: Okuma Hachitarô, whom we had not met before, assured us that he knew all about the subject, for he had read the Bible
entries.source_note: Satow (1921), ch. XXXI.

entries.headline: Looking back: the protests had little effect
entries.digest: In the same passage Satow summed up the outcome. The foreign diplomats' joint protests did little, and the government went on to exile some four thousand people of all ages and both sexes, mostly from Urakami. His figure is a round number from memory, higher than the later official count.
entries.quote: the measure of exiling to other parts of the country some four thousand Japanese
entries.form: memoir (written later) based on his diaries
entries.source_note: Satow (1921), ch. XXXI.

entries.headline: The order for exile
entries.digest: An administrative order of the new government directed that the Urakami Christians be handed to domains across Japan. The order covered about 4,010 people, to be distributed among some thirty domains. The first group to leave would be the leaders.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia chronology (7 June); Burkman 1974 (8 June, 4,010 to 33 domains).

entries.headline: Exile in Tsuwano
entries.digest: Tsuwano received its first group of 28 Urakami Christians in mid-1868 and held them at a site designated for followers of a heterodox creed. Takagi is generally counted among the leaders sent there. The villagers came to call the whole ordeal the tabi, the 'journey'.
entries.source_note: Christian Today (2015) on Tsuwano's first 28; MLIT R1-00790 on 'tabi'. Takagi's destination not confirmed from his own text.

entries.headline: Kido sends 114 leaders away
entries.digest: Kido came to Nagasaki, where the new governor Sawa Nobuyoshi and Inoue Kaoru had investigated the village. He approved sending 114 of the leading Urakami Christians to the domains of Hagi, Tsuwano and Fukuyama. The rest of the village was left, for the moment, in place.
entries.source_note: MLIT R1-00790 and 001561261; date per Wikipedia chronology.

entries.headline: 4,010 sentenced, 120 already sent
entries.digest: Passing on the Nagasaki consuls' correspondence, Van Valkenburgh reported the sentences of banishment and hard labour and that 120 had already been sent away. About 16 death sentences had been commuted, which he credited to foreign pressure. He advised that the powers should do no more than keep urging a more humane policy.
entries.quote: four thousand and ten native Christians had been ordered to be punished by banishment and hard labor
entries.source_note: FRUS 1868 pt I, doc. 361.

entries.headline: A draft letter urging milder measures
entries.digest: Nakai Hiroshi showed Satow a draft letter from Komatsu Tatewaki to Kyoto about the treatment of the Nagasaki Christians. Satow noted that it took up Parkes's arguments for gentler handling. Inside the government, not everyone favoured the hard line.
entries.form: memoir (written later) based on his diaries
entries.source_note: Satow (1921), late chapters.

entries.headline: The whole village is summoned and shipped away
entries.digest: According to a Japanese official memorandum later forwarded by De Long, every Urakami household was summoned on 1 January to appear the next morning, given a three-day delay, and the removal was finished by 8 January. The memorandum said families were kept together where possible and property auctioned, and blamed the hardships on cold and mud. About thirty people fled.
entries.form: translated official memorandum in a dispatch
entries.source_note: FRUS 1870, doc. 286 (dispatch of 12 April 1870).

entries.headline: Gotō numbers and the government's reassurance
entries.digest: De Long sent home the Japanese replies to the consuls' protests. They reported more than a thousand Christians on the 'Soto' islands (probably the Gotō group), of whom 335 had recanted, 593 were confined and 140 had escaped, and denied severe cruelty. Of the 700 Urakami men being deported, Japan promised they would be given into the care of several domain lords.
entries.quote: those people will not be subject to any severe labor.
entries.source_note: FRUS 1870, doc. 282.

entries.headline: Parkes: you are oppressing them for our faith
entries.digest: Speaking for all the foreign representatives at a conference with the prime minister, Iwakura and the foreign ministers, Parkes repeated that persecution for religion would offend every treaty power. He framed the villagers as people who shared the faith of the foreign nations. The Japanese ministers gave no promise to change course.
entries.quote: You are oppressing them because they profess the faith that we do, and this must be offensive to us.
entries.source_note: FRUS 1870, doc. 282, enclosure 1.

entries.headline: Sanjō: not their faith, their disobedience
entries.digest: Opening the conference, Sanjō stated that the government was not moving the villagers because of their religion. He said they were being removed because they had long been ungovernable and insubordinate. The same act was thus described in two incompatible ways in a single document.
entries.quote: This government does not move these people on account of their religious professions
entries.source_note: FRUS 1870, doc. 282, enclosure 1.

entries.headline: News of the deportation reaches Parliament
entries.digest: Asked in the Commons about Christians expelled from Nagasaki, the under-secretary for foreign affairs replied that the report was substantially correct. He said Parkes had protested at Nagasaki and then in the capital with a joint note, but that orders to halt came too late. About 2,800 had been deported and some 200 allowed to stay.
entries.source_note: Hansard, HC Deb 18 March 1870, vol. 200 cc203-4.

entries.headline: An official account no one has contradicted
entries.digest: De Long forwarded the Japanese memorandum on the deportation, which he thought was written by the officers who carried it out. It claimed nobody was arrested and that the villagers had come of their own accord. De Long noted only that the account had not been challenged, and that the government's aim was to stop conversions.
entries.quote: Whether true or not, this report as yet stands uncontradicted.
entries.source_note: FRUS 1870, doc. 286.

entries.headline: The question becomes international correspondence
entries.digest: From London the US minister Motley sent Washington ten enclosures from Lord Clarendon on the alleged persecution of converts in Japan, including British and French papers. The exiles were now a subject of exchange between foreign ministries on three continents. None of the papers came from the exiles themselves.
entries.source_note: FRUS 1870, doc. 289 (Motley to Fish, 2 June 1870).

entries.headline: News in Rome, and a return
entries.digest: Petitjean, in Rome for the Vatican Council, learned there of the mass exile of Urakami. He returned to Japan in December 1870 to find the village emptied of its Christian families.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia chronology.

entries.headline: An inspection brings some relief
entries.digest: By then 153 Urakami Christians had been sent to Tsuwano in two groups, and dozens had died, some after confinement in tiny punishment cages. An official of the foreign ministry inspected the domain in May 1871, and treatment improved afterwards. In all, Tsuwano is remembered for 37 deaths among the exiles.
entries.source_note: Christian Today (2015), Tsuwano series; numbers as given there.

entries.headline: Abroad, the exiles block treaty revision
entries.digest: Wherever the Iwakura Mission went, Western governments and church groups raised the treatment of Japanese Christians. The persecution became one of the obstacles to the treaty revision the mission wanted, and messages went home urging a change. Kido and his colleagues were meeting abroad the consequences of the policy he had helped carry out in 1868.
entries.source_note: MLIT 001561262; Wikipedia chronology; Breen (1998).

entries.headline: Kume sees Christianity as a public religion
entries.digest: In New York the mission visited the American Bible Society and the YMCA and were given Bibles printed in Chinese. Kume's record observed that Americans used their faith to judge moral character, which the envoys found hard to accept, yet he concluded that it bound the society together and reached ordinary people more easily than Confucianism. At home, the same faith was still on the notice boards as a crime.
entries.source_note: Kume, Bei-Ō kairan jikki vol. 19 (New York), as summarised by History of Japanese in NY; date of the visit approximate.

entries.headline: Those who stayed hidden by choice
entries.digest: Not every hidden community joined the Church once it was legal. Some, later called Kakure Kirishitan or hanare ('separated') Christians, kept their own leaders, prayers and calendars, from fear of new trouble and loyalty to what their ancestors had kept. The concealed way had become a tradition of its own, distinct from the Catholicism the missionaries brought.
entries.source_note: Burkman 1974 n. 22; Japan Past & Present (Gotō oral-history project); MLIT 001561260 on the threefold division.

entries.date_display: 24 February 1873 (Meiji 6; Gregorian calendar now in use)
entries.headline: The notice boards come down
entries.digest: Dajōkan Proclamation No. 68 ordered the removal of the public notice boards, including the one banning Christianity. The ban itself was not formally repealed; the government explained that the notices were already widely known. In practice, open Christian worship would be tolerated.
entries.source_note: MLIT 001561262; National Archives of Japan record cited in Wikipedia; Christian Today (2015).

entries.headline: Order to send the exiles home
entries.digest: A Dajōkan directive ordered the domains, now prefectures, to return the 'heterodox' believers of Nagasaki to their homes. The returns took months. Of about 3,394 exiled, some 613 were recorded as dead.
entries.source_note: MLIT R1-00790 and 001561262; Christian Today (2015).

entries.headline: Coming back to a village that was theirs again
entries.digest: Survivors began to return from Tsuwano in May 1873, and groups came back by ship from Kagoshima and elsewhere through the year; one ship carried 330, including 13 children born in exile. They found fields gone to waste and houses sold. Takagi lived in Urakami until his death in 1899.
entries.source_note: Christian Today (2015); Wikipedia chronology (Kagoshima Maru); return totals differ between sources.

convergences.label: Disclosure at Ōura
convergences.note: The only record of the moment is the outsider's; the woman who took the risk is known through his letter and later tradition.

convergences.label: The night raid on Urakami
convergences.note: The magistrate counts criminals; Takagi's memorandum later tells it as a confession of faith; the American minister hears of it secondhand and calls it the governor's own act.

convergences.label: Reprieve under the old regime
convergences.note: France wins a release under surveillance; the American legation passes on the priests' complaint that the promised releases had not happened; the prisoners are bound to recant or watched.

convergences.label: The Osaka week: notice boards argued over
convergences.note: Parkes speaks of civilisation, Ōkuma of public order, Satow writes both down, and the council that decides on exile has already met.

convergences.label: The first deportation
convergences.note: An order in Kyoto, Kido's arrangements in Nagasaki, a number in a US dispatch, and the leaders' journey into exile.

convergences.label: The mass removal and the Tokyo conference
convergences.note: One protocol holds two irreconcilable descriptions of the same act; De Long forwards both, and a Japanese memorandum denying force, without judging between them.

convergences.label: The boards come down
convergences.note: A government decree at home, pressure felt abroad by the Iwakura Mission, and the exiles' slow return to Urakami.

ties.note: She spoke to him in the Ōura church on 17 March 1865; he wrote the only contemporary account.
Takagi's house held one of the secret chapels the priests visited by night.
The magistrate's raid of July 1867 arrested Takagi with the others.
Okabe's 1856 arrests were the 'third' crackdown; Tokunaga's raid became the fourth, the Yonban Kuzure.
The American minister confirmed the arrests with Petitjean and forwarded his letter to Washington.
The priests were French; Roches's intervention with the shogun was made on the mission's behalf.
Satow was Parkes's interpreter at the Osaka meetings of May 1868.
They argued the Christian question face to face at Osaka in May 1868.
Their words of 19 January 1870 stand side by side in the same protocol.
De Long joined the joint protest and the conference of January 1870 in which Parkes spoke for the foreign representatives.
Both travelled with the Iwakura Mission, Kido as vice-ambassador and Kume as its recorder.
Kido arranged the 1868 deportation of the leading Urakami Christians.
Kido was among the ministers at the Nishi Hongwanji meeting Satow described.

threads_out.note: The Urakami Cathedral built by the returned exiles and their children stood near the hypocentre of the Nagasaki atomic bomb on 9 August 1945 and was destroyed with much of the Catholic community of Urakami.

The treaties that followed Perry's 1853–54 visits opened Nagasaki as a treaty port and allowed the Ōura church to be built for foreigners, the setting for the 1865 disclosure; the Sotome tradition of confessors arriving on black ships was read in that light.

The same Meiji government that removed the notice boards in February 1873 had switched Japan to the Gregorian calendar weeks earlier, ending the lunisolar calendar by which the hidden communities had kept their feast days.

images.title: Image to Trample On (Fumi-e): Madonna of the Immaculate Conception
images.caption: A small bronze tablet set in wood, used in the annual e-fumi tests in which residents of Nagasaki stepped on a Christian image to prove they were not Christians. Kept in the Nagasaki magistrate's storehouse until the Meiji era.
images.credit: Tokyo National Museum, via Cultural Japan (CC BY 4.0)

images.title: Fumie (Image to trample on): Madonna and Child (Madonna of the Rosary)
images.caption: Another trampling image from the Nagasaki magistrate's collection; such objects, and the registers of who had stepped on them, were the official record that concealment was working.
images.credit: Tokyo National Museum, via Cultural Japan

images.title: Fumi-e: wooden plaque with a copper figure of Christ crowned with thorns
images.caption: A trampling plaque reproduced from N.H.N. Mody's 1969 collection of Nagasaki prints; the catalogue dates the e-fumi practice from the early 17th century to about the 1850s.

images.title: Ōura church, photographed c. 1865, with the 1926 illustration of the confession of faith
images.caption: The Japan Tourism Agency commentary reproduces Ueno Hikoma's early photograph of Ōura church with its tenshudō sign, Furet's architectural drawing and Aimé Villion's 1926 illustration of the 17 March 1865 scene (an imagined picture made sixty years later).
